title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Power Plants | MPI, US
description: Magnetic particle inspection of boiler, HRSG, B31.1 piping, turbine and hydro parts at US power plants: surface crack checks on welds. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Power Plants: MPI of Welds, Repairs and Rotating Equipment
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection (MT, also called MPI or mag particle testing) on ferritic steel welds, repairs and forgings at US power plants. Typical jobs are pressure part attachment welds on boilers and HRSGs, B31.1 steam piping repairs, turbine casing and bolting, and hydro gate and runner components. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and report to your inspector. Request an MT inspection quote with the component list and outage dates.

Why magnetic particle inspection matters at a power plant

Most cracking in power equipment starts on a surface: at the toe of a weld, in the root of a fillet, at a sharp change of section or where grinding left a gouge. Thermal cycling, vibration and corrosion fatigue all work from the outside in. MT is the standard way to find those cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel because it is fast, it shows the indication directly on the part, and it detects flaws too tight for the eye. A magnetic field is induced in the part, fine iron particles are applied, and a crack that interrupts the field draws them into a visible line.

It is a surface and near-surface method. It does not measure wall loss and it does not find deep internal flaws, which is why plants pair it with ultrasonic work; see our page on ultrasonic testing for power plants. It also only works on ferromagnetic material. Austenitic stainless steel lines and nonferrous parts need liquid penetrant testing for power plants instead. The national overview is on our magnetic particle testing page.

Boilers, HRSGs and pressure part repairs

Boilers built to ASME Section I and maintained under the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC) see constant weld repair. After a tube panel replacement, a header stub repair or a nozzle build-up, the surface of the finished weld is typically examined by MT before any hydrostatic test. The same applies to attachment welds that carry load: tube supports, lugs, seal bars and spacer ties, which crack when the tube they are attached to moves. In combined cycle plants, HRSG modules cycle faster and harder, and attemperator, drum nozzle and header-to-tube welds are common examination points. Surface cracks in those welds are far easier to find with MT than by any visual check through scale.

Where a defect has been ground out, MT confirms the excavation is clear before the welder fills it, and again after the weld is finished and ground. That sequence is written into most repair plans and we follow whichever sequence your repair procedure sets. The state boiler inspector or authorized inspection agency decides what examination is required; Atlantis provides the method and the record.

B31.1 piping, supports and bolting

Power piping is built to ASME B31.1, which sets examination requirements for fabrication welds and permits owners to add more for service. MT applies to ferritic socket and butt welds, branch connections, support attachments and the pipe hangers and constant-support hardware that can crack from overloading. Stud and bolt threads on flanges and valve bonnets are also examined when the joint is opened and the owner wants a surface check before reassembly. Our weld inspection page describes how MT fits into a full weld examination scope.

Where there is pipe in the scope, MT is often combined with the thickness work described in ultrasonic pipe thickness testing: a technician reads wall thickness at the elbow and then checks the adjacent weld in the same visit.

Turbines, generators and castings and forgings

Steam turbine casings, valve bodies, rotor and shaft sections, and large flanges are castings or forgings, and their cracks are almost always surface-breaking. When the turbine service provider or owner needs a surface check after a repair or at an inspection, MT is the typical method. Our job page, magnetic particle inspection of castings and forgings, describes technique for those shapes. Generator retaining rings and some rotor components are controlled by the original manufacturer's requirements, and those requirements take precedence over anything on this page.

On hydropower projects, MT is used on gate components, wicket gate linkages, runner repairs and structural steel attachments to penstocks. Access is often the hardest part, because these parts sit in wet, dark and confined locations that the owner has to make safe.

Technique: yoke, prods, wet and dry

Technique is chosen for the part. A hand-held AC electromagnetic yoke is the workhorse for field work; ASME Section V Article 7 requires it to lift a defined test weight, and we check lifting power with the test block before use. Yokes are preferred on pressure parts because they do not arc to the surface. Prods, which pass current through the part, can leave arc burns and are restricted or prohibited on many pressure parts by owner specification, so we use them only where the written procedure and the owner allow.

Dry powder works well on rough or warm surfaces such as as-welded or hot-service steel, while wet fluorescent particles under black light give the highest sensitivity on smooth ground surfaces and in shaded areas. We measure ultraviolet intensity and ambient white light at the work, as the practice requires. Field direction matters: every area is examined in two directions about ninety degrees apart because a crack parallel to the field will not show. Surface temperature limits depend on the particle carrier; we state the allowed range in the procedure. Our explainer on ASME Section V Article 7 goes through these requirements, and the complete MT guide covers the physics.

Surface preparation and what limits a good result

MT does not need a perfectly clean part, but it does need a surface free of loose scale, heavy rust, weld spatter and thick coatings that hold particles away from a crack. On boiler and piping welds we clean to bare metal with a wire brush or flap disc, and a thin paint film is tolerated only when the procedure has been demonstrated through it. Peened or smeared metal from aggressive grinding can close a crack mouth, so where a repair has been dressed hard, a light etch or fresh surface is sometimes needed before the examination. Tell us how the surface will be left when we arrive, and we will say whether any preparation falls in our scope.

Codes and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 7 governs the method, and ASTM E709 describes the practice. Acceptance criteria are not in Section V; they come from the construction or repair code, such as ASME Section I or B31.1, or from the owner's specification. For repairs under the NBIC, the repair plan and the authorized inspector define the criteria. Linear indications above the allowed length are rejected; rounded indications are evaluated by size and spacing. In every report we state the criteria used. When the required acceptance standard is unclear, we ask your inspector rather than guess.

What the report contains

  • Plant, unit, system and component identifiers tied to your drawings
  • Procedure number and revision, and the governing code or specification
  • Equipment: yoke or prod, particles, carrier and lifting power or field checks
  • Surface preparation and condition, temperature and lighting measurements
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Each indication with location, orientation, length and accept or reject
  • Sketches or photographs showing coverage and any limitations

A Level II performs and interprets; an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. Atlantis reports the indications and the criteria used. We do not repair welds, decide fitness for service or act as the authorized inspector.

What to send for a quote

  • Component list, drawings or weld maps, with quantities
  • Material grade and thickness, and surface temperature during work
  • Governing code, repair plan or owner specification, with acceptance criteria
  • Surface condition: as-welded, ground, coated or insulated
  • Access: scaffold, lift, confined space and permits
  • Outage dates, badging or background check requirements and the site address

Planning for outages and repairs

MT work often lands late in a repair sequence, after welding and grinding, and it can hold up the next step. Tell us which repairs will need examination and whether re-examination after rework is likely. Power plants regularly require site orientation, lockout and tagout, and sometimes screening before access; give us the requirements at quoting so the right people are mobilized. Wet particle work in a dim area needs dark conditions for black light and can conflict with welders working nearby, so schedule it with the area owner. Atlantis does not arrange scaffold, lifts or rope access.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because it is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules. We do not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B qualification and do not work on safety-related nuclear components. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page. We do not calculate remaining life, assess fitness for service or act as inspector of record; your engineer or authorized inspector does that with our data.

Where we work in the US for power generation

  • Charlotte: gas-fired and converted units across the Carolinas with frequent weld repair.
  • Knoxville: hydro and fossil stations across the Tennessee Valley.
  • Atlanta: Southeastern combined cycle plants and their HRSG attachment welds.
  • Birmingham: Alabama steam plants and heavy steel fabricators nearby.
  • Phoenix: Southwestern peaking units where start-stop cycling cracks welds.
  • Chicago: Midwestern generation and district steam plants.
  • Pittsburgh: Ohio River Valley stations and forging and casting shops.
  • Columbus, Ohio: Central Ohio plants with frequent boiler repair scopes.

Training your own MT technicians

Plants that want routine MT in house can start with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. The power generation NDT training page covers plant-specific topics, and the magnetic particle simulator lets trainees practice yoke technique and indication reading. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so we can help with a written practice for your site. For procedure work, see NDT technical procedure development. When a part might be MT or PT, our MT versus PT comparison helps you decide.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless steel steam piping?
faq.a: No. MT only works on ferromagnetic material, and austenitic stainless steel is not magnetic. For stainless lines, nickel alloys and other nonferrous parts we use liquid penetrant testing, which finds surface-breaking cracks regardless of magnetism.

faq.q: Which power plant components get MT most often?
faq.a: Weld repairs and attachments on boilers and HRSGs, B31.1 piping welds and supports, turbine casing and valve castings, bolting and hydro gate and runner components. The common theme is ferritic steel with a surface crack concern.

faq.q: Do you use prods on pressure parts?
faq.a: Only if your specification and our written procedure allow it. Prods can leave arc burns, so many owners restrict them on pressure parts. We default to an AC yoke on boilers and piping.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the indications?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria come from the construction code, repair plan or owner specification, such as ASME Section I, B31.1 or an NBIC repair document. We state the criteria in the report; your authorized inspector or engineer makes the final decision.

Within the limits of the particles and carrier. Dry powder tolerates higher temperature than wet suspension, and the procedure states the maximum surface temperature. We examine at a safe temperature agreed with your inspector.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT on an outage scope?
faq.a: Component list or weld maps, material and thickness, code or repair plan with acceptance criteria, surface condition, access arrangements, outage dates, badging requirements and the site address. Quantities help us size the scope.

faq.q: Do you provide the authorized inspector for boiler repairs?
faq.a: No. The authorized inspector or state boiler inspector stays your appointment. Atlantis supplies the magnetic particle examination and a report that the inspector can review against the repair plan.

faq.q: Is MT or UT better for finding cracks in a weld?
faq.a: MT is more sensitive to surface-breaking cracks on ferritic steel, and UT is needed for internal flaws and wall thickness. Many repair plans call for both. Tell us the concern and we will recommend the sequence.

faq.q: Do you work on nuclear plants?
faq.a: Not on safety-related equipment. Atlantis does not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B qualification, so any scope that requires it is outside our work. Secondary-side or other balance-of-plant parts are considered only when the owner's program accepts our written practice.
